691.quote_or_event: “The kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs; they go out and awaken the sleeping people to harass them.”
691.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the rulers and officials of his day as predators whose power falls unpredictably on ordinary people.
691.tie_back: The Kural warns that changeable, powerful kings must be approached like a fire, neither too near nor too far; Guru Nanak's tigers make the same point about the danger of royal power, though from the side of its victims.
691.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
691._accuracy_note: Partial and partly contrasting: both see royal power as dangerous, but Guru Nanak condemns it rather than teaching courtiers how to live safely near it.

692.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
692.explanation: Guru Nanak makes coveting and taking what is another's due as abhorrent as the gravest taboo of one's own faith.
692.tie_back: The Kural tells the servant not to covet what the king himself desires; Guru Nanak's rule against taking what belongs to another covers that case as a general principle.
692.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
692._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a general ban on taking another's due, not prudent restraint before a king, and the Kural's promised reward of lasting royal favour has no parallel.

693.quote_or_event: “Why do you do such evil deeds, that you shall have to suffer so? Do not do any evil at all; look ahead to the future with foresight.”
693.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak warns against any deed whose consequences one will later have to bear, urging foresight before acting.
693.tie_back: The Kural advises guarding against grave faults because a ruler's suspicion, once roused, cannot be undone; Guru Nanak likewise counsels avoiding wrong entirely by looking ahead to its consequences.
693.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
693._accuracy_note: Next-best only: shares the advice to avoid faults with foresight, but has nothing on the irreversibility of a ruler's suspicion.

694.quote_or_event: “It is not good to slander anyone, but the foolish, self-willed manmukhs still do it.”
694.explanation: Guru Amar Das condemns slander and talk behind others' backs as the habit of the self-willed (manmukh).
694.tie_back: The Kural forbids whispering in another's ear or sharing private smiles in the presence of the great; Gurbani's ban on backbiting covers the moral side of such whispering, though not its court etiquette.
694.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
694._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sikh scripture has no teaching on courtly decorum; this matches only the idea that private whispering about others is wrong.

695.quote_or_event: “His limits cannot be perceived. What is the Mystery of His Mind?”
695.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak says the purposes in the mind of the divine King cannot be pried into or exhausted by human effort.
695.tie_back: The Kural tells the courtier not to strain after the king's secret counsel but to hear it only if the king reveals it; Guru Nanak treats the Lord's counsel as a mystery beyond human probing, known only as He reveals it.
695.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 24), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
695._accuracy_note: Next-best only: an analogy from the divine King to an earthly one; Japji speaks of God's unknowable will, not a courtier's discretion about state secrets.

696.quote_or_event: “So what offering can we place before Him, by which we might see the Darbaar of His Court? What words can we speak to evoke His Love? In the Amrit Vaylaa, the ambrosial hours before dawn, chant the True Name, and contemplate His Glorious Greatness.”
696.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak asks how one should approach the divine Court and with what words, and answers with the right time (the hours before dawn) and the right speech (the True Name and His praise).
696.tie_back: The Kural says to read the king's mood, wait for the right moment and then say what he will want to hear; Guru Nanak's question and answer about approaching the heavenly Court turn on the same two things, timing and welcome words.
696.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 4), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
696._accuracy_note: Strong structural fit (court, timing, words that win love), but the King is God and the 'right words' are devotion, not tactful counsel to a ruler.

697.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
697.explanation: Closing a hymn on the violence of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak insists on telling the truth about rulers and events, whatever the powerful might prefer to hear.
697.tie_back: The Kural tells the counsellor to say only what is truly good for the king and never what is useless, even if the king asks for it; Guru Nanak's resolve to speak only truth at the decisive moment rests on the same integrity.
697.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
697._accuracy_note: Partial: shares the refusal to trade truth for what pleases, but Guru Nanak speaks as a prophet about rulers, not as a courtier advising one.

698.quote_or_event: Amar Das (born 1479) became the disciple of Guru Angad (born 1504), a man twenty-five years his junior, and after Guru Angad's death succeeded him as the third Guru at the age of 73.
698.explanation: Sikh tradition remembers Amar Das for years of humble service to his younger Guru, to whose family he was also related by marriage, treating him with full reverence as Guru.
698.tie_back: The Kural forbids slighting a ruler on the grounds that 'he is younger than me' or 'he is my relative', and asks respect for the dignity of the office; Amar Das honoured a younger Guru, and a kinsman, entirely for the light of the office he held.
698.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Amar Das and Guru Angad (dates and succession)
698._accuracy_note: Strong fit on both excuses the Kural names; Britannica supports the ages and succession, while the details of his service and the marriage link come from Sikh tradition as reported on Wikipedia, and the relationship is Guru and disciple rather than king and courtier.

699.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, one who claims to know everything shall not be decorated in the world hereafter.”
699.explanation: At the end of Japji Pauri 21 Guru Nanak warns that the self-important person who presumes on his own greatness is not honoured in the Lord's Court.
699.tie_back: The Kural says that people of steady judgement never presume on the king's favour to do what he would not accept; Guru Nanak likewise warns that presumption (haumai) loses honour in the Court one thinks one has a claim on.
699.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
699._accuracy_note: Next-best only: shares the warning against presumption before a sovereign, but Japji's context is claiming to know God's greatness, not presuming on royal favour.

700.quote_or_event: According to Sikh tradition, Guru Angad's son Datu, resenting that Amar Das had been made Guru, came to Goindwal, taunted him that only yesterday he had been a water-carrier in their house, and kicked him from his seat; Amar Das humbly asked whether he had hurt his foot, withdrew for a time, and Datu, finding no following, went back to Khadur.
700.explanation: Datu relied on his old family standing and familiarity with the new Guru to act with contempt, and lost all standing as a result.
700.tie_back: The Kural warns that the familiarity which says 'we are old acquaintances' and then behaves improperly brings ruin; Datu's appeal to old household ties to justify his insult is exactly that, and it left him without followers.
700.source: Wikipedia, Guru Amar Das (citing Sikh tradition)
700._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on familiarity turning into contempt and self-ruin, but it is a traditional account sourced from Wikipedia as a last resort, and the 'ruin' is loss of standing rather than destruction.
